title: Write a query to find customers (or users) who have BOTH state A and state B (e.g. a completed AND a cancelled order) using conditional aggregation in one grouped pass.
shortTitle: Customers With BOTH State A and State B — Conditional Aggregation
topicTitle: Aggregation — GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT, SUM

s1_definition.profdef: To find entities that have at least one row of state A and at least one row of state B, you group by the entity and use conditional aggregation in the `HAVING` clause: `HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END) > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 END) > 0`. This does it in one grouped pass over the table, avoiding two separate queries intersected together.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants customers who have both a completed order and a cancelled order — a signal worth investigating. Priya groups all orders by customer, and for each customer she asks two questions in one pass: "does this customer have at least one completed order?" and "at least one cancelled order?" Only customers who answer yes to both make the list. Counting the completed ones and the cancelled ones separately within the same group is conditional aggregation.
s1_definition.oneliner: Group by the customer and use `HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status='A') > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status='B') > 0` — both states proven in a single pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** To find entities that have at least one row of state A and at least one row of state B, you group by the entity and use conditional aggregation in the `HAVING` clause: `HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END) > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 END) > 0`. This does it in one grouped pass over the table, avoiding two separate queries intersected together.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants customers who have both a completed order and a cancelled order — a signal worth investigating. Priya groups all orders by customer, and for each customer she asks two questions in one pass: "does this customer have at least one completed order?" and "at least one cancelled order?" Only customers who answer yes to both make the list. Counting the completed ones and the cancelled ones separately within the same group is conditional aggregation.

**One line to remember:** Group by the customer and use `HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status='A') > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status='B') > 0` — both states proven in a single pass.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach runs two queries — "customers with a completed order" and "customers with a cancelled order" — and intersects them, or uses two `EXISTS` subqueries. That works but scans the table multiple times. Conditional aggregation does it in a single grouped pass, which is cleaner and usually faster.

The technique puts a `CASE` expression inside an aggregate. `COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END)` counts only the rows where the condition is true, because `CASE` returns `NULL` otherwise and `COUNT` ignores NULLs. So within each customer's group, this expression tells you how many completed orders they have:

```sql
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END) > 0
   AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 END) > 0;
```

`GROUP BY customer_id` makes one group per customer, the first conditional count must be above zero (at least one completed order exists), and the second must be above zero (at least one cancelled order exists). The `AND` requires both, so only customers satisfying both states survive. This reads the table once.

You can equivalently use `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` or, in PostgreSQL, the compact `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'COMPLETED')`, which is the modern standard-SQL filtered aggregate and reads very clearly:

```sql
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'COMPLETED') > 0
   AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'CANCELLED') > 0;
```

The same pattern generalizes nicely. "Customers with A but NOT B" becomes `HAVING COUNT(... A ...) > 0 AND COUNT(... B ...) = 0`. "Customers with all of A, B and C" just adds more conditions. "At least two of three states" can use a sum of booleans. This flexibility is why conditional aggregation is preferred over intersecting multiple queries once you need anything beyond the simplest case.

Senior nuances: the conditional counts can also be projected in the `SELECT` to report how many of each state a customer has, which the two-query approach cannot do in one shot. Watch the difference between `COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END)` (counts matching rows) and `COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` (counts all rows, because 0 is not NULL) — the `ELSE 0` version is wrong for counting and must be paired with `SUM`, not `COUNT`. For performance an index on `(customer_id, status)` supports the grouping and the conditional filters. And when status values come from user input, keep them controlled (an enum or lookup) so the CASE conditions stay reliable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India's risk team wants to flag customers who have both a COMPLETED order and a CANCELLED order, because that pattern can indicate testing stolen cards (complete one, cancel another) and warrants a review. Rajesh (SAV2001) has one completed and one cancelled order — he should be flagged. Priya (CUR3001) has two completed orders but no cancellation — she should not. An earlier approach ran two separate queries and intersected them in application code, which was slow and hard to extend when risk added a third state.

This exercises conditional aggregation in a single grouped pass. Our mini-project models an `Order` with a status, a repository, and a `RiskReviewService` that returns customers having both states using one pass of conditional counts.

The code will contain: an `Order` class with a `status`, an `OrderRepository`, a `RiskReviewService.customersWithBothStates()` method implementing the conditional-aggregation HAVING logic, and a `Demo` printing the flagged customers.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four orders — SAV2001 has one COMPLETED and one CANCELLED; CUR3001 has two COMPLETED.

Step 1: The service groups orders by customer, preparing a two-slot counter per customer: one slot for state A (COMPLETED) and one for state B (CANCELLED). This is the `GROUP BY customer_id` plus the two conditional counts.

Step 2: It scans every order once. SAV2001's COMPLETED order increments slot A to 1; SAV2001's CANCELLED order increments slot B to 1. CUR3001's two COMPLETED orders increment its slot A to 2, leaving its slot B at 0. This single pass is exactly what `COUNT(CASE WHEN ...)` does inside one aggregation.

Step 3: It applies the HAVING test: keep customers where both slots are above zero. SAV2001 has A=1 and B=1, so both are positive and he is flagged. CUR3001 has A=2 and B=0, so the cancelled condition fails and she is not flagged.

Step 4: The flagged list contains only SAV2001. Note the table was read just once — no intersection of two separate queries.

Step 5: The application prints SAV2001 for the risk team to review.

```
Oct 25, 2026 16:57:10 WARNING: Customers with BOTH COMPLETED and CANCELLED: [SAV2001]
CUSTOMERS WITH BOTH COMPLETED AND CANCELLED:
  SAV2001
```

```
  └──────────────────┘
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find customers who have both state A and state B I group by the customer and use conditional aggregation in the HAVING clause, so the whole thing is one grouped pass over the table: `SELECT customer_id FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END) > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 END) > 0`. The trick is that the CASE returns NULL when the condition is false and COUNT ignores NULLs, so each conditional count tallies only the rows of that state within the customer's group. Requiring both counts to be above zero means the customer has at least one of each. On PostgreSQL I prefer the clearer `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'COMPLETED')` filtered aggregate.

In our National Bank of India risk program we flag customers who have both a completed and a cancelled order, because that combination can indicate card testing. Rajesh had one completed and one cancelled order so he was flagged, while Priya had two completed and no cancellation so she was not. The earlier approach ran two separate queries and intersected them in application code, which was slow and hard to extend; the conditional-aggregation version reads the table once and is trivially extensible. The senior points I add are that the pattern generalizes — "A but not B" is one count above zero and the other equal to zero, "all of A, B and C" just adds conditions — and that I can also project the per-state counts in the SELECT to report how many of each, which two separate queries cannot do in one shot. I also watch the difference between COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END) and the ELSE 0 variant, and I index on customer and status. The line I remember is: group by the entity and HAVING a conditional count of each state above zero, all in a single pass.

---

keyPoints: GROUP BY: group rows by column values
Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
HAVING: filter groups (vs WHERE which filters rows)
GROUP BY + HAVING vs WHERE: WHERE runs first, HAVING runs after grouping
